Mount Ephraim
EE-fray-im
proper noun (place)
Hebrew har Ephrayim; the central hill country of the tribe of Ephraim, the setting of many events in Israel's history.

📖 Biblical Definition

Mount Ephraim, the hill country of the tribe of Ephraim, was the central highland region of Israel, the scene of a great many events through the periods of Joshua, the Judges, and the kingdom. There Joshua received his inheritance and was buried (Josh 24:30); there Deborah the prophetess dwelt and judged Israel under her palm tree (Judg 4:5); there lay Shiloh, where the tabernacle long stood, and Ramah, the home of Samuel; and there too occurred the idolatry of Micah and the dark events of the Levite's concubine in the days when there was no king in Israel (Judg 17-19). The hill country of Ephraim was thus a region of both faithful service and grievous failure, a microcosm of Israel's history. Its highlands held the heart of the nation's life and worship for generations. Mount Ephraim stands in the dictionary as the central hill country of Israel, a witness to the mingled record of God's people — the burial-place of the faithful Joshua and the seat of Deborah's judgeship, yet also the scene of idolatry and lawlessness when every man did what was right in his own eyes — and a reminder that the same land may hold both the noblest faith and the darkest sin, as the heart of the covenant people swung between devotion and apostasy.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The central hill country of the tribe of Ephraim, the setting of many events: Joshua's burial (Josh 24:30), Deborah's judgeship (Judg 4:5), Shiloh and Ramah, and the idolatry and lawlessness of Judges 17-19.

MOUNT EPHRAIM, proper noun. The central hill country of the tribe of Ephraim.

Where Joshua received his inheritance and was buried (Josh 24:30).

Where Deborah the prophetess judged Israel under her palm (Judg 4:5).

Containing Shiloh (the tabernacle) and Ramah (Samuel's home).

The scene also of Micah's idolatry and the Levite's concubine (Judg 17-19).

📖 Key Scripture

Josh 24:30 — "And they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnathserah, which is in mount Ephraim, on the north side of the hill of Gaash."

Judg 4:5 — "And she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment."

Judg 17:6 — "In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes."

1 Sam 1:1 — "Now there was a certain man of Ramathaimzophim, of mount Ephraim..."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Mount Ephraim needs no defense from redefinition; its mingled history witnesses that the same people and place may hold both noble faith and grievous sin, and that the heart swings between devotion and apostasy.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sober honesty of Scripture about God's people. Mount Ephraim held the grave of faithful Joshua and the seat of Deborah's wisdom, yet also Micah's idol-shrine and the lawless horrors of Judges 19. The dictionary holds that the Bible does not whitewash the covenant people: the same land and nation that produced great faith also fell into deep apostasy, and the record stands as both encouragement and warning, that we presume not, but take heed.

No-king note. The dark events in mount Ephraim are framed by the refrain, "In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 17:6). The dictionary holds the lesson: where there is no acknowledged rule of God and His law, men descend into idolatry and lawlessness, each becoming his own authority. The remedy is the rightful King, foreshadowed in Israel's monarchy and fulfilled in Christ, under whose righteous reign alone the heart finds its true order.
